note: One entry per code (SPEC §20.3-20.4). {name} is filled from the fault's facts. Fixes list the no-terminal way first (D22); a command is something the person copies and runs themselves, with what it does and how to undo it (D49, D53). Sources: the 2026-09-29/30 case on the Mint box (journal), Debian/Ubuntu/Mint documentation as cited per fix.

G101.title: The graphics driver is installed but not running
G101.meaning: The NVIDIA driver ({driver}) is installed, but it isn't loaded for the running kernel ({kernel}). The screen falls back to a basic mode and the assistant can't use the graphics card.

causes.unsigned: Secure Boot is on and the driver isn't signed with a key this computer trusts.
causes.not_built: The driver was never built for kernel {kernel}.
causes.file_damaged: The driver file for kernel {kernel} reads back damaged. That usually means the disk or its connection had trouble, not the driver itself.
causes.driver_refused: The driver started but refused to run (see the evidence).
causes.unknown: The cause isn't one this tree knows yet; the evidence is recorded in full.

unsigned.words: Let the driver's key be enrolled at the next start.
steps: Open Driver Manager and reinstall the recommended driver; it asks for a one-time password.
Restart. A blue screen titled "Perform MOK management" appears: choose Enroll MOK, Continue, Yes, type that password, then Reboot.
unsigned.verify: the driver loads after the restart (nvidia-smi shows the card)

not_built.words: Build the driver for this kernel.
steps: Open Driver Manager, pick the recommended driver again, click Apply Changes, then restart.
not_built.command: sudo apt install linux-headers-{kernel} && sudo dkms autoinstall -k {kernel}
not_built.explain: Installs the kernel's build files and builds every add-on driver (here: NVIDIA) for kernel {kernel}. Changes only driver files for that kernel.
not_built.undo: Nothing to undo: it builds what should have been there.
not_built.verify: dkms status lists {module} as installed for {kernel}

file_damaged.words: First make sure the disk is healthy (ask: is my disk OK?). Then put a fresh copy of the driver in place.
file_damaged.explain: Builds the NVIDIA driver again for kernel {kernel} and replaces the damaged copy. Nothing else changes.
file_damaged.undo: Nothing to undo: it's the same driver version.
file_damaged.verify: after a restart, nvidia-smi shows the card

driver_refused.words: Start the previous kernel, which worked, while this is looked into.
steps: Restart. When the menu appears (hold Shift, or tap Esc, while the computer starts), choose Advanced options, then the older kernel.
driver_refused.verify: the driver loads on the older kernel

unknown.words: Start the previous kernel, and share the report (cinminai-diag report) with whoever helps.

S301.title: An installed kernel has no graphics driver
S301.meaning: Kernel {kernels} is installed but the NVIDIA driver isn't built for it. Starting that kernel would leave the screen in basic mode.

causes.not_built: The driver wasn't built when the kernel was installed (missing build files, or the build failed).

not_built.words: Build the driver for that kernel before restarting into it.
not_built.command: sudo apt install linux-headers-{kernel} && sudo dkms autoinstall -k {kernel}
not_built.explain: Installs the kernel's build files and builds the NVIDIA driver for kernel {kernel}. Nothing changes for the kernel you're running now.
not_built.verify: dkms status lists the driver as installed for {kernel}

I301.title: A disk's connection is reporting errors
I301.meaning: The connection to {disk_words} failed {exceptions} times: commands sent to the disk failed ({failed}) and the link was reset. The errors point at {signal}. Failed writes can leave files damaged.

causes.one_kernel: It happens with kernel {kernels_bad}, not with {kernels_clean}. Newer kernels send bigger pieces of data at a time (failed pieces here: up to {largest_failed_kib} KiB); an older disk or a borderline cable can choke on them.
causes.every_kernel: It happens with every kernel, so it's the hardware: the cable, the port, the power plug, or the disk.

one_kernel.words: Switch to the kernel that works (Update Manager, View, Linux kernels). Until then, make this kernel send smaller pieces to the disk, the way older kernels do.
one_kernel.explain: Limits each write to {disk} to 1280 KiB (it's {max_sectors_kb} now). Nothing is written to the disk by this. It lasts only until the next restart, so don't restart after it.
one_kernel.verify: no new errors for the disk in the next heavy copy or update
one_kernel.source: Linux block layer (queue/max_sectors_kb); the 2026-09-30 case, PLAN D52

every_kernel.words: Check the disk's own health record, then the cable.
steps: Open Disks, choose the disk, open the menu (⋮) and choose SMART Data & Self-Tests.
If "UDMA CRC Error Count" goes up over a few days: replace the SATA cable and use another port.
If reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sectors go up: the disk is wearing out. Copy your important files elsewhere now.
every_kernel.verify: no new link errors after the change

I302.title: Writing to the disk failed
I302.meaning: Some writes to the disk failed{aborted_words}. Files written at that time may be damaged, and the system may switch the disk to read-only to protect it.

causes.write_errors: Writes failed because the disk's connection had errors.
causes.read_only_now: The system disk ({device}) is read-only right now: nothing can be saved, updates and drivers can't install, and USB sticks show as read-only too.

write_errors.words: Copy your important files somewhere safe, then let the disk check run at the next start.
steps: Restart normally (from the menu, not the power button).
If a text screen ends with (initramfs), type the command below and press Enter, then type exit.
write_errors.explain: Checks and repairs the disk's filing records. It can't bring back the contents of files that weren't written; reinstall or re-copy those.

read_only_now.words: Don't keep working on a read-only disk. Restart from the menu so the disk check can run.
steps: Save what you can to a USB stick on another computer if it matters.
Restart from the menu. If the (initramfs) screen appears, type the command and press Enter, then exit.
read_only_now.explain: Checks and repairs the disk's filing records at start.
read_only_now.verify: after the restart, saving a file works

S401.title: The problems follow one kernel
S401.meaning: Kernel {kernel} had problems in {bad_boots} of {boots_on_kernel} starts; kernel {good_kernels} had none on this computer. A newer kernel isn't always better for older hardware.

causes.kernel_regression: Something in kernel {kernel} doesn't suit this computer.

kernel_regression.words: Switch to the long-term kernel, without the terminal.
steps: Open Update Manager, then View → Linux kernels.
Install the long-term kernel series (on Mint 22: 6.8, supported to 2029), or keep {good_kernel}.
Remove kernel {kernel} in the same window, then restart.
kernel_regression.verify: uname -r shows the kernel you chose, and the problems are gone
kernel_regression.source: Linux Mint user guide, Update Manager; the 2026-09-30 case

kernel_regression.words: For one start only: pick the kernel at the start menu.
steps: Restart. Hold Shift (or tap Esc) while the computer starts, choose Advanced options, then {good_kernel}.
kernel_regression.explain: Shows which kernel is running now. It only reads.

H401.title: The computer didn't shut down cleanly last time
H401.meaning: The last session ({ended}) ended without a shutdown: a crash, a power cut, or the power button held down. That can damage files that were being written.

causes.unclean: The previous session's record stops without a shutdown.

unclean.words: When the computer freezes, try the keyboard before the power button.
steps: Press Ctrl+Alt+F3 for a text screen; log in and type sudo reboot.
If even that doesn't respond: hold Alt and SysRq (Print Screen) and press, slowly, R E I S U B — a safe forced restart.
A short press of the power button asks the system to shut down cleanly; only holding it cuts the power.
unclean.source: Linux kernel documentation, sysrq; the 2026-09-29 case

I101.title: A system service failed
I101.meaning: These services failed to start or stopped with an error: {units}.

causes.failed_unit: A service reported a failure; its own log says why.

failed_unit.words: Look at the service's own message.
failed_unit.explain: Shows whether the service runs and its last log lines. It only reads.

S101.title: An update was left unfinished
S101.meaning: The package database says an installation didn't finish (for example after a power cut during an update).

causes.interrupted: An install or update was interrupted.

steps: Open Update Manager: it offers to fix it.
interrupted.explain: Finishes setting up packages that were unpacked but not configured. It doesn't download or remove anything.

P101.title: The processor got too hot
P101.meaning: The processor reached its temperature limit {count} times and slowed itself down to cool off. The computer feels slow when that happens, and heat can make it freeze or switch off.

causes.throttled: Not enough cooling: dust in the fans or vents, a blocked air path (a laptop on a soft surface), a fan that stopped, or dried-out thermal paste.

throttled.words: Give it air, and clean the cooling.
steps: Put a laptop on a hard, flat surface; keep the vents free.
With the computer off and unplugged: blow the dust out of the vents and fans (short bursts of compressed air; hold the fan still).
If it keeps happening: a fan may have stopped, or the thermal paste may need renewing. That's a job for a repair shop or a confident tinkerer.
throttled.verify: no new overheating messages under the same work

P301.title: The hardware reported an error
P301.meaning: The processor reported {count} hardware errors (machine checks). They can come from unstable power, memory, the processor itself, or settings like overclocking.

causes.hardware_error: A hardware fault the processor caught: most often memory, power, heat, or an overclock.

hardware_error.words: Test the memory, and undo any overclock.
steps: Restart and choose Memory test in the start menu (or from the Cin-MinAI USB stick); let it run a full pass.
If the computer's settings (BIOS) have an overclock or memory profile (XMP/EXPO) turned on, try it off.
If errors continue with everything at standard settings: the power supply or the processor may be failing.

P302.title: The computer ran out of memory
P302.meaning: Memory ran out {count} times and the system closed a program to keep going: {details}.

causes.out_of_memory: More was open than the memory holds: many browser tabs, a big program, or a large AI model.

out_of_memory.words: Keep fewer big things open at once.
steps: Close tabs and programs you aren't using; System Monitor (in the Menu) shows what uses the most memory.
If it's the assistant's model: choose a smaller one, or let it unload when idle.
If it happens often: more memory (RAM) is the lasting fix.
out_of_memory.verify: no programs closed for lack of memory

G102.title: The graphics card or its driver reported a problem
G102.meaning: The graphics card hung or stopped responding {count} times (NVIDIA codes: {xids}). The screen freezes when that happens.

causes.fell_off_bus: The card dropped off its connection to the computer (NVIDIA Xid 79). On a desktop that's usually power (the supply or its cables) or heat; sometimes the card's slot.
causes.hang: The graphics card stopped answering and was reset. It can be a driver bug, heat, or an unstable overclock.
causes.driver_message: The NVIDIA driver reported an error (code {xids}) that doesn't by itself mean the card stopped: often a program's own fault, or the driver being unloaded at shutdown. Once is usually harmless; it matters if it repeats while you work.

fell_off_bus.words: Check the card's power and seating.
steps: Turn the computer off and unplug it. Reseat the graphics card and its power cables (all of them, firmly).
Make sure the power supply is strong enough for the card; avoid splitters and adapters.
Check the card's fans spin and the case has airflow.
fell_off_bus.verify: no new 'fallen off the bus' messages under load
fell_off_bus.source: NVIDIA Xid documentation; Netdata guide to Xid 79

hang.words: Update or change the driver, and rule out heat.
steps: Open Update Manager and install the updates; then Driver Manager: try the recommended driver.
If it started after a kernel update: start the previous kernel (Advanced options in the start menu).
Undo any graphics overclock; check the card's fans.

driver_message.words: Nothing to do unless it repeats while you work; then update the driver.
steps: If the screen froze or a program closed at that moment: open Update Manager and install the updates, then check Driver Manager for the recommended driver.

B301.title: The kernel hit an internal error
B301.meaning: The kernel (the core of the system) reported an internal error {count} times. A crash or freeze can follow.

causes.kernel_error: A bug in the kernel or a driver, or a hardware fault it ran into.

kernel_error.words: If it started after an update, go back to the kernel that worked; then share the report.
steps: Restart, open Advanced options in the start menu, and choose the previous kernel.
Save the report (cinminai-diag report) and share it when you ask for help: the evidence lines are what helpers need.

N101.title: Wi-Fi is switched off
N101.meaning: The Wi-Fi ({names}) is switched off, so no networks show up.

causes.hard: A physical switch or a key (often Fn with an antenna symbol) turned the Wi-Fi off. Software can't turn it back on.
causes.soft: It's turned off in the system: airplane mode, or Wi-Fi switched off in the network settings.

hard.words: Turn the Wi-Fi switch or key back on.
steps: Look for a Wi-Fi switch on the side or front, or a key with an antenna symbol (often pressed together with Fn).
Some laptops have it in their settings (BIOS) instead.
Click the network icon in the panel (bottom right) and switch Wi-Fi on; turn airplane mode off if it's on.
soft.explain: Turns the Wi-Fi radio back on (only the software switch).
soft.undo: rfkill block wifi turns it off again.

N102.title: The Wi-Fi card has no working driver
N102.meaning: This computer has Wi-Fi hardware ({hardware}), but the system made no Wi-Fi device from it, so there's no Wi-Fi.

causes.firmware: The card needs a firmware file the system doesn't have: {firmware}.
causes.driver: The card has no driver in this system (some need one installed separately).

firmware.words: Get the missing firmware with the updates.
steps: Connect with a cable (or a phone's USB tethering) for a moment.
Open Update Manager and install all updates: newer firmware comes with the linux-firmware package.
If it's still missing: Driver Manager may offer a driver; otherwise the card may need a newer kernel (Update Manager, View, Linux kernels).
firmware.verify: Wi-Fi networks show up after a restart

steps: Connect with a cable or a phone's USB tethering for a moment.
Open Driver Manager: it lists drivers for hardware that needs one.
If none is offered, ask with the report: the card's name tells helpers which driver it needs.
driver.source: Linux Mint user guide, Driver Manager

D301.title: A Windows drive opens only for reading
D301.meaning: The Windows drive {device} was left marked as "in use" (dirty), so Linux opens it read-only, or not at all, to protect your files.

causes.windows_fast_startup: Windows' Fast Startup (on by default) doesn't fully shut Windows down: it leaves its drives marked as in use. A Windows crash or hibernation does the same.

windows_fast_startup.words: Shut Windows down fully, and turn off Fast Startup.
steps: Start Windows. Open Control Panel, Power Options, Choose what the power buttons do, Change settings that are currently unavailable, untick Turn on fast startup, Save.
If Windows asks or the drive still won't open: in Windows, run the disk check (This PC, right-click the drive, Properties, Tools, Check).
Shut Windows down (not restart into Linux from hibernation), then start Cin-MinAI.
windows_fast_startup.verify: the drive opens with write access
windows_fast_startup.source: ntfs3 driver behaviour; Manjaro NTFS primer; Microsoft Fast Startup

D302.title: A USB device keeps failing to connect
D302.meaning: A USB device on port {details} failed to connect or lost its connection {count} times.

causes.wire_errors: The signal on the USB wire was garbled: often a worn cable, a loose port, a hub without enough power, or the device itself.

steps: Plug the device straight into the computer (not through a hub), in another port; on a desktop, use a port at the back.
Try another cable, especially for phones and external disks.
For an external hard disk: use its own power supply if it has one.
wire_errors.source: USB error -71 (EPROTO): Linux USB documentation, Arch forums

I303.title: The disk is (nearly) full
I303.meaning: {mount} has {free_gb} GB free of {size_gb} GB ({free_pct} %). When it's full, updates fail, programs can't save, and logging in can fail.

causes.nearly_full: Files have built up: downloads, videos, old system snapshots, or cached updates.
causes.full: It's full: save nothing important until space is freed.
causes.boot_full: The small boot area is full of old kernels, so kernel updates can't install.

steps: Open Disk Usage Analyzer (in the Menu) to see what takes the space; the biggest folders are usually Videos, Downloads and Pictures.
Empty the Trash.
If Timeshift keeps snapshots on this disk, delete older ones in Timeshift.
nearly_full.source: Linux Mint user guide; Ubuntu documentation, disk usage

steps: Empty the Trash, and move large videos or downloads to a USB disk.
Delete old Timeshift snapshots in Timeshift if it stores them here.
full.explain: Deletes downloaded update files that are already installed. It removes no programs or settings.
full.undo: Nothing to undo: they're downloaded again if ever needed.

steps: Open Update Manager, View, Linux kernels, and remove kernels older than the two newest (keep the one you're running).
boot_full.source: Linux Mint user guide, Update Manager

S102.title: Some packages are broken
S102.meaning: Some installed packages have dependencies that aren't met, so installs and updates stop until it's fixed.

causes.broken_dependencies: An install was interrupted, or a package from outside the normal sources needs something it can't get.

broken_dependencies.words: Let the package manager repair it.
steps: Open Update Manager: it often offers to fix this itself.
broken_dependencies.explain: Installs what's missing (or removes what can't work) so the packages fit together again. It lists everything before it asks you to confirm.
broken_dependencies.undo: Read the list before you type Y: anything it would remove can be installed again later.

U201.title: A service in your session failed
U201.meaning: These parts of your desktop session stopped with an error: {units}.

causes.failed_unit: A background part of your session (sound, the keyring, a helper) failed; its own log says why.

failed_unit.words: Log out and back in; if it repeats, look at its message.
failed_unit.explain: Shows whether it runs and its last log lines. It only reads.

S601.title: No automatic system snapshots
S601.meaning: Timeshift, which can take you back to a working system after a bad update, isn't set to take snapshots by itself.

causes.not_set_up: Timeshift hasn't been set up yet.
causes.no_schedule: Timeshift is set up, but no schedule is on.

steps: Open Timeshift from the Menu and follow its setup: RSYNC, a disk with room (another disk is best), and daily plus boot snapshots.
Your personal files aren't included by default; it protects the system.

no_schedule.words: Turn on a schedule in Timeshift (recommended, your choice).
steps: Open Timeshift, Settings, Schedule: tick Daily and Boot.

causes.crashed: A program hit an error it couldn't recover from. Once can be a bug; repeated crashes of many programs can point to memory or the disk.

crashed.words: Open it again; if it keeps crashing, update it.
steps: Install the updates in Update Manager.
If many different programs crash: test the memory (Memory test in the start menu).

X101.title: The assistant's model server crashed
X101.meaning: The program that runs the assistant's model crashed in {boots_n} starts (kernel {kernels}), so the assistant couldn't answer then.

causes.with_disk_errors: It crashed in starts where files were read back damaged or the disk had errors: a damaged read of the model file fits. The disk and kernel findings are the cause to fix.
causes.crashed: It crashed for a reason the record doesn't show; the assistant's own log has more.

with_disk_errors.words: Fix the disk or kernel problem first; the assistant comes back with it.
with_disk_errors.verify: the assistant answers after a restart

crashed.words: Restart the assistant; if it repeats, share the report.
crashed.explain: Starts the assistant again (and its model server with it).
